items.title: Qube ($60bn) is building a US options market-making desk — and the hard part is adverse selection, not pricing
items.idea: Qube Research & Technologies (~$60bn AUM) is seeking a US broker-dealer licence for options market making with 25 NY hires (FT, Nov 25). OCC data: options ADV 70.9M contracts YTD, +18% y/y, but growth is lopsided — ETF options +34.3% vs single-stock options +5.5%. The core point: a quote at $2.04 that gets lifted before mid moves to $2.10 is a 6c ($6/contract) adverse markout — you get filled most when you're most wrong, so spread × volume wildly overstates the economics.
items.angle: Another multi-strat moving into flow internalization = more competition for retail/ETF options flow, compressing PFOF-style economics. Watch $HOOD $CBOE $IBKR volume-vs-capture dynamics.
items.tweetA: ETF options volume +34% this year. Single-stock options +5.5%. The 0DTE/ETF complex is where the growth is — and now a $60bn quant shop wants a seat at the table. Edge in market making isn't the model, it's surviving the fills you get when you're wrong.
items.tweetB: Everyone multiplies spread × volume to value market makers. Wrong math. The trades you win are disproportionately the ones that move against you 10 seconds later. That's why only firms with Jane Street-level compute budgets keep winning this game.

items.title: Backtests lie when fills are modelled independently of price moves — exchange allocation rules belong inside the sim
items.idea: Cites Lalor & Swishchuk 'Market Simulation under Adverse Selection' (2026): simulations on CME futures overstate performance when executions are modelled independently from subsequent price moves. Cboe BZX Options is price-time while C2 is pro-rata — so quoted size has different value per venue, and bigger size also means bigger accumulated exposure in a sudden move. Optiver: one underlying can expose hundreds of linked quotes; risk is set by how fast mass-cancel messages reach the exchange.
items.angle: Market-structure plumbing piece — useful framing for why HFT/options-MM profits concentrate in a few firms with infra scale (links to AI Street record revenues item).
items.tweetA: The most expensive bug in quant isn't a wrong forecast. It's a backtest that assumes you'd have been filled at your quote. The fills you'd actually get are the ones that hurt.
items.tweetB: Price-time vs pro-rata matching sounds like trivia. It decides whether quoting bigger size is free money or a loaded gun when the underlying gaps. Microstructure is where the alpha hides.

items.title: Bitcoin back near $60K and 'has yet to find a bottom' — the recovery never fixed underlying dynamics
items.idea: Ecoinometrics argues the multi-month BTC recovery was never accompanied by a change in underlying market dynamics, so it stayed fragile and vulnerable to reversal. Now back around $60K after a technical breakdown, with weak on-chain activity and persistent ETF withdrawals offering 'little reassurance'. Their positioning stance remains defensive (detail paywalled).
items.angle: Third crypto-bearish source in the window (with News Block and Capital Wars liquidity) — consensus is now uniformly defensive, which is itself a contrarian signal to monitor.
items.tweetA: BTC at $60K with persistent ETF outflows and weak activity. The rally earlier this year was price without participation. Those always round-trip.
items.tweetB: When the quant crypto shops, the macro liquidity guys and the Bitcoin podcasters all say 'no bottom yet' on the same day — I start building a list of what would prove them wrong.

items.title: Claims 189k, core PCE 3.3% — and the Fed wants to hike again into an AI-trade breakdown
items.idea: Initial claims fell to 189k from 202k (11k below consensus); continuing claims 1.697M after 1.792M (holiday seasonals distort). Purchase mortgage apps +10.2% w/w at a 7.38% 30-yr rate. Oct PCE headline and core +0.3% m/m, 3.8% and 3.3% y/y. Boockvar: the Fed wants another hike in a few weeks 'as the AI tech trade breaks down' — the AI trade being the main driver of both the economy and high-income spending via the wealth effect.
items.angle: Policy error setup: hiking into a wealth-effect shock. Front-end vol and curve flattener trades; links to Capital Wars 'devil's cross'.
items.tweetA: Core PCE 3.3%. Claims 189k. On paper the Fed has every reason to hike. In reality the top 10% of earners drive spending, and their wealth just took a Nasdaq -4% gap. Hiking into that is how you turn a correction into a recession.
items.tweetB: 30-yr mortgage at 7.38% and purchase apps still jumped 10%. Either housing demand is far stickier than anyone modeled — or this is holiday seasonal noise. My bet: noise. Watch next week's print as the 10-yr decline flows through.

items.title: Pre-market: SPX futures -2.1%, NDX -3.2%, crude $82.66 — plus a wall of single-name signals
items.idea: Futures at time of writing: SPX -2.13%, Nasdaq -3.17%, crude $82.66 (+1.2%). Core PCE 3.3% y/y vs 3.2% expected (headline in line at 3.8%). Raymond James reiterates Strong Buy and $350 PT on NVDA but lists overhangs: next week's congressional hearings, board investigation, succession, customer financing. Trump told NY Post a Huang pardon is 'an option' and told CNBC he's open to a US government equity stake in Nvidia.
items.angle: Government-equity-stake-in-NVDA talk is a regime change for the stock's risk premium — state-capitalism discount or put? Positioning into next week's hearings.
items.tweetA: President says a pardon for Nvidia's CEO is 'an option' and he's open to a government equity stake. The world's most important chip company now trades on political risk like a Chinese SOE. Price that.
items.tweetB: Raymond James keeps $350 on $NVDA while listing congressional hearings, a board investigation, succession and customer financing as overhangs. That's four binary events. The PT is the least informative number in that note.

items.title: CoreWeave 5y CDS at 13.14% = ~68% implied 5-yr default probability; Alphabet CDS at a record too
items.idea: CoreWeave 5-year CDS hit a record 13.14%, implying a 68% chance of default within five years (S&P Global). CRWV 2032 notes fell 4.6 points to a record-low 74.9c; shares -11.9%. The cost to insure Alphabet's debt also hit a record overnight, alongside Oracle and SpaceX, as AI credit fears spread.
items.angle: AI credit contagion moving up the quality stack — from neoclouds (CRWV) to ORCL to GOOGL. The CDS market is front-running equity. Watch HY tech spreads and GPU-backed ABS.
items.tweetA: $CRWV CDS at 13.14%. The bond market is pricing a two-in-three chance CoreWeave defaults within five years. The equity is still worth billions. One of these markets is very wrong.
items.tweetB: When Alphabet — net cash, a money printer — gets its CDS to a record in the same week as CoreWeave, credit isn't pricing default. It's pricing the end of 'capex at any cost'. That's an equity multiple problem, not a solvency one.

items.title: Meta's Muse took 51% of agentic orders in one week; Microsoft declares 'Code Red' after historic outage
items.idea: Meta brought its Muse AI assistant into Instagram DMs (US, Canada, Mexico, Japan, Singapore); Forter data shows Muse accounted for 51% of agentic orders in the week ending Nov 22, and Meta says Muse, though ad-free, raises advertiser conversions. Separately, Microsoft declared an internal 'Code Red' after this month's outage, targeting worldwide critical fixes within one hour. Amazon launched 36 Leo satellites on Ariane 6 (network ~432) after a ULA Vulcan failure destroyed 40.
items.angle: Agentic commerce share is consolidating fast in whoever owns the messaging surface — $META could be the default agentic checkout. MSFT reliability becomes a competitive issue for Azure AI.
items.tweetA: Meta's AI assistant did 51% of all agentic orders last week, one week after landing in Instagram DMs. Agentic commerce won't be won by the best model. It'll be won by whoever owns the chat window you're already in. $META
items.tweetB: Microsoft 'Code Red' after an outage while everyone is migrating critical workloads to agents running on its cloud. Reliability is the next AI moat nobody's pricing.

items.title: 84% of UK historians study regions holding 16% of humanity — a structural blind spot in expertise
items.idea: Clossey & Guyatt found 84% of historians in surveyed UK history departments worked on Britain, Europe or North America — leaving 16% to cover regions with 84% of the world's population. Despite predictions global history would fade after Brexit/Trump 2016, Journal of Global History submissions rose 123% between 2016 and 2025. Frankopan argues the distribution of academic expertise shapes what governments and businesses can understand about the world.
items.angle: Talent/knowledge gap with real consequences: Western institutions under-resourced on the Middle East, South/Southeast Asia, Africa — exactly where geopolitical and growth risk concentrates.
items.tweetA: 84% of UK historians study places where 16% of humanity lives. Then we're surprised when Western governments and investors misread India, the Gulf and Africa. Expertise allocation is a geopolitical risk.
items.tweetB: Everyone said 'global history had its moment' after 2016. Submissions to the field's main journal then rose 123%. Deglobalization didn't kill interest in the world — it made understanding it more valuable.

items.title: JPMorgan AM 2027: slowdown without recession, 1-2 more Fed hikes then extended pause
items.idea: J.P. Morgan Asset Management's 2027 Year-Ahead Outlook (David Kelly, Gabriela Santos) expects the US to slow without recession, inflation to retreat, and the Fed to move to an extended pause after one or possibly two more hikes. The tension: a still-growing economy, an expensive bond market, and earnings expectations 'anything but modest' must all coexist. Concentration flagged as a key 2027 risk; opportunities seen beyond US tech.
items.angle: Consensus house view is soft landing + more hikes; that's a narrow path. Positions: international/value diversification, short-duration bias.
items.tweetA: JPM's 2027 base case: no recession, inflation down, 1-2 more hikes, then pause, and earnings stay strong. Every one of those has to go right simultaneously. That's not a base case, it's a parlay.
items.tweetB: The interesting line in the big-bank 2027 outlooks isn't the S&P target. It's that concentration is now officially a top risk. When the sell side says diversify out of US tech, they're telling you where the flows go next.

items.idea: Bitcoin fell to ~$55K over the weekend — lowest in 2+ years — bounced above $60K, then slid again as the Nasdaq dropped 4% at the open. Record-pace BTC ETF outflows in November; BTC trades below its 200-week moving average. Oct CPI +0.4% m/m, core +0.3% for three straight months; the 2025 shutdown left a gap so no y/y could be computed (last annual 3.7%).
items.angle: A lifelong BTC bull calling 'lower from here' is notable sentiment capitulation. 200WMA loss is the historical cycle-low zone.
items.tweetA: BTC below the 200-week average. Historically that zone has been where cycle lows get carved, not where they start. The question is whether ETF holders have the stomach that 2018 and 2022 OGs did.
items.tweetB: Fun fact buried in the CPI report: the government literally couldn't compute year-over-year inflation because the 2025 shutdown left a hole in the data. We're setting rates on incomplete numbers.

items.title: 'People thought Bitcoin would change their lives — then AI actually did' — AI capex as a capital vacuum
items.idea: Investor Eric Weiss (early Saylor confidant, involved with Core Scientific — ex-BTC miner now building AI data centers) argues Bitcoin's frustrating 2026 is an AI story: the capital needed to build AI pulled money from almost everything else. He sees parts of AI as a bubble and expects capital to flow back once it shakes out. Also: one-party championing of Bitcoin triggers reflexive opposition from the other.
items.angle: Capital-rotation framing links crypto weakness to AI capex. If AI credit cracks (CRWV CDS), does the money come back to BTC or to cash?
items.tweetA: Best explanation of 2026 crypto I've heard: Bitcoin was supposed to change people's lives, then AI actually did, and sucked every marginal dollar into data centers. If AI capex breaks, BTC isn't hedged against it — it's the next bid.
items.tweetB: Bitcoin miners became AI data center landlords. Their equity now trades on GPU lease rates, not hashprice. The 'Bitcoin infrastructure' trade quietly became an AI credit trade. $CORZ $IREN

items.title: 'Devil's cross' on the yield curve — first major signal since late 2021
items.idea: Howell: weakening Global Liquidity drives the turbulence, now spreading to economic activity. The US curve is flattening while CrossBorder's convexity measure rises (curve flatter and more humped). The rising convexity line crossing above the falling slope line = 'devil's cross'; the previous major one was late 2021. Sequence: Bitcoin fell first, then gold, now stocks. He reads Huang's reinstatement as 'a potentially desperate attempt to restore confidence'.
items.angle: Late-2021 analog = start of the 2022 bear. Bond-market signal > equity narrative. Watch for liquidity stabilization before re-risking; 2H27 rebound per Howell.
items.tweetA: The last time this yield-curve 'devil's cross' fired was late 2021. What came next was 2022. Bonds are saying the same thing again while equities argue about Jensen.
items.tweetB: Liquidity unwind order this cycle: Bitcoin first, then gold, now stocks. The most liquidity-sensitive asset leads. If you want to know when it ends, watch BTC turn first — not the Nasdaq.

items.title: HRT $21.4B, Jane Street >$40B, Citadel Securities >$15B — all beat full-year records with a quarter to spare
items.idea: HRT posted $21.4B revenue in 9M 2026 vs $12.3B for all of 2025. Citadel Securities passed its full-year record with >$15B. Jane Street hit >$40B by mid-August vs $39.6B all last year. Jane Street committed ~$19B to compute this year; XTX switched on the first of five Finnish data centers. Speed edge is near the speed-of-light limit, so firms push into 'mid-frequency' (seconds to minutes) where the trade-off is speed vs model intelligence.
items.angle: Vol is a revenue engine for the non-bank liquidity providers; their compute spending is an underappreciated source of AI demand that is countercyclical to equity drawdowns.
items.tweetA: Jane Street made more by mid-August than in all of 2025 — $40B+. Then committed $19B to compute. When the market's most profitable trading firm spends half its revenue on GPUs, AI demand isn't just hyperscalers.
items.tweetB: HRT's revenue went from $12.3B to $21.4B in nine months. Every selloff is a transfer from discretionary humans to the firms with the most compute. Volatility is their product, and 2026 is a bumper crop.

items.title: DRW opens to outside money for compute + crypto; Jump runs a compute trading desk
items.idea: DRW plans to manage outside capital for the first time, targeting compute and crypto, with products in early 2027 (Bloomberg). DRW and Jump both backed GPU pricing provider Silicon Data; Itô Markets founders now lead Jump's compute trading desk. Leopold Aschenbrenner (Situational Awareness): 'One person on our team spent two million dollars on tokens last month.'
items.angle: Compute is becoming a tradable commodity with prop-shop market makers — GPU forward curves and derivatives incoming. $2M/month in tokens per analyst is a demand datapoint for inference.
items.tweetA: A hedge fund analyst spent $2M on AI tokens in one month. That's a whole research team's salary — on inference. Token demand from finance alone could rival a mid-size cloud customer.
items.tweetB: Crypto trading firms are now building GPU compute desks and raising outside money for it. Compute is becoming the next commodity with a forward curve. Whoever prices it, owns the spread.

items.title: FCA warns AI agents may need authorisation; ECB to pilot AI inspections; Citadel Sec cuts data review 40h→2h
items.idea: UK FCA warned tech companies their AI agents may need authorisation if they offer financial services; UK regulators published AI cyber-risk practices (limit agent permissions). ECB plans pilot inspections of how banks oversee AI. Citi cautioned customers against third-party AI agents. Citadel Securities cut new-dataset evaluation from 40 hours to 2 with agents, added 50% more datasets y/y; compute hours up 20x since 2021. FT: AI server suppliers raising prices up to 45% after deals signed.
items.angle: Agentic finance regulation is arriving in Europe first. Server price hikes of up to 45% post-contract = supply-chain pricing power, margin pressure for neoclouds.
items.tweetA: FCA: if your AI agent moves money, it may need a licence. The agentic commerce trade just met financial regulation. Europe regulates first, the US copies later.
items.tweetB: AI server suppliers are raising prices up to 45% after contracts are signed. Meanwhile CoreWeave CDS implies 68% default odds. The supply chain has pricing power; the renters don't. That's the whole AI credit story.

items.title: 'The new AI narrative' — debt on debt, one stock, an Anthropic IPO into chaos, and the President as board
items.idea: Greenberg: Monday's 'AI narrative is back' rally fully reversed; the new narrative is how overextended the trade was — debt piled on debt, hanging on Nvidia. Anthropic ($ANT) IPO launched into a highly volatile market ('the biggest IPO known to mankind'), raising the question what OpenAI does now. Trump pressured Nvidia's board to reinstate Huang while the question of chips sold to China via Singapore remains unresolved.
items.angle: Governance-discount framing for NVDA; IPO supply ($ANT) absorbing AI-equity demand at the worst time. OpenAI's window may be closing.
items.tweetA: Anthropic got its IPO done into a 4%-down Nasdaq. Smart. The window is closing, and the question now is whether OpenAI can go out at all. The last mega-IPO of a cycle usually marks the top.
items.tweetB: Reinstating a CEO under presidential pressure while the China-via-Singapore chip question is unresolved isn't a governance footnote. It's an export-control tail risk now attached to the market's bellwether. $NVDA

items.title: A Georgia city manager's 1,974 ChatGPT sessions: AI wrote the laws, the council voted 3-0
items.idea: Hsieh filed 150+ records requests to 120+ local governments; Kingsland, GA (pop ~20k) city manager handed over 1,974 ChatGPT sessions (Nov 2023-Sep 2026). ChatGPT wrote most of the city's data center ordinance from a DeKalb template (passed 3-0), a Title VI policy from one prompt, and a backflow ordinance + fee schedule + guide in ~3 minutes via 'yes' replies to its own offers. The water superintendent didn't recognize the $50 inspection fee and called the $25 annual registration fee 'a mistake'. 40%+ of US public sector employees used AI at work in 2025 (from 28% in Q2 2024).
items.angle: 'Offer-acceptance loop' — model proactivity as a mechanism for AI drifting into governance. Regulatory risk for data center siting: AI-drafted ordinances skipping legally required hearings.
items.tweetA: The scariest word in this story is 'yes'. ChatGPT offered to draft a fee schedule, the city manager typed 'yes' in 40 seconds, the council passed it. Nobody chose the $25 fee. It just appeared.
items.tweetB: An AI-written data center ordinance referenced 'Heavy Industrial' zones the city doesn't have and skipped a legally required public hearing. That procedural hole is what let a Navy base and a riverkeeper stall a 700-acre data center park. AI governance risk is now siting risk.

items.title: Navy sub base + riverkeeper unite to stall a 700-acre data center park — local backlash gets new allies
items.idea: Eleven days after Kingsland passed its data center ordinance, a developer moved to rezone ~700 acres of former timberland for an industrial park allowing data centers. The commanding officer of Kings Bay Naval Submarine Base and St. Marys Riverkeeper both backed tabling the rezoning; the city later passed a one-year data-center moratorium. Ordinance also gave the city manager power to waive closed-loop cooling requirements.
items.angle: Military + environmental coalitions against data centers is a new siting headwind, esp. near bases. Water/cooling rules are the battleground. Bullish for sites with existing industrial zoning and power.
items.tweetA: When a nuclear submarine base commander and an environmental riverkeeper are on the same side, your data center isn't getting built. The AI power trade keeps assuming sites are infinite. They aren't.
items.tweetB: One-year data center moratorium in a 20,000-person Georgia town. Multiply by every county with a water table and a vocal riverkeeper. Permitted, powered land is the real scarce asset in AI.

items.title: Gold -34% peak-to-trough this year vs only -14% in the 2018 'autopilot QT' episode
items.idea: Some compare gold's 2026 to 2018 when Powell's tightening was 'on autopilot'. But gold fell only ~14% from its early-2018 peak — a blip compared to this year's 34% peak-to-current-trough drawdown. Includes a 2018-2019 gold price chart.
items.angle: Scale of the gold drawdown exceeds any tightening analog — this is a liquidation/margin event (matches Capital Wars sequencing BTC→gold→stocks). The 2018 analog also implies the eventual 2019 rebound.
items.tweetA: Gold is down 34% from the peak. In 2018, with QT on autopilot, it fell 14%. This isn't a rates story. It's forced selling from people who needed liquidity — and gold was the only thing still bid.
items.tweetB: Everyone's using 2018 as the gold analog. Remember what happened after: the Fed pivoted in Jan 2019 and gold ripped. If the Fed hikes once more into an AI unwind, the pivot that follows could be bigger.

items.title: Anthropic rewrote the API serving every Claude token from Python to Rust in ~5 months, humans read ~20% of the code
items.idea: The Messages API (auth, tokenization, billing, safety checks) was a Python monolith; a few engineers with no Rust experts rewrote it in ~5 months, verified by shadowing production traffic until responses were identical. Engineers closely reviewed only ~20% of generated code. Driver: CPU footprint amid a 'global CPU shortage'. Anthropic is now public at ~$1T market cap with about a tenth of the headcount of similarly valued companies.
items.angle: CPU shortage is the underpriced AI bottleneck (bullish $AMD $INTC $ARM server CPUs). Verification-by-shadowing is the template for AI-led legacy migrations — huge for COBOL/mainframe modernization.
items.tweetA: Anthropic rewrote its core API in Rust with no Rust experts, reading only 20% of the code, because a CPU shortage made Python too expensive. AI isn't just GPU demand. It's making CPUs scarce too. $AMD $ARM
items.tweetB: $1T market cap with a tenth of the headcount of its peers. If that ratio holds, the revenue-per-employee chart of 2030 looks nothing like today's. Every legacy software company should be modelling that.

items.title: Anthropic dropped the coding interview because strong candidates kept failing it — they no longer write code by hand
items.idea: Code-review classifier decides if a PR needs human review, how many reviewers and which team; low-risk changes are reviewed and merged by another Claude. A Claude agent triages API on-call alerts before humans are paged. Onboarding is 'talk to Claude'. Two-pizza teams (5-8) persist; planning/alignment time unchanged — engineers spend more time coordinating than implementing. Coding interviews phased out; 'time to complete a project' is now meaningless for promotions, replaced by measured impact.
items.angle: Labor-market signal: hiring screens, promotion metrics and team structure are being rebuilt. The constraint moves from implementation to coordination — management/PM roles become the bottleneck.
items.tweetA: Anthropic killed the coding interview because the best candidates kept failing it. They don't hand-write code anymore. LeetCode prep is officially a stranded asset.
items.tweetB: Inside the most AI-native company on earth: implementation is nearly free, but planning and alignment take as long as ever. The bottleneck in an AI economy isn't writing code. It's humans agreeing on what to build.

items.title: 'The industry that creates a technology rarely captures its value' — rotating from semis to downstream
items.idea: Market Sentiment rotated out of memory/advanced packaging/optics in September; SOXX is down 27% since. YTD: their portfolio +22% vs NDX +4%, SPX +5%. Nvidia closed +31% on Monday's Huang reinstatement, which they use to finish exiting semis. Thesis: AI price per performance fell ~1,000x in three years; value moves downstream. 25 S&P 500 companies said AI lifts margins by 180bp on average; Waste Connections' AI pricing tool adds ~$20M/yr EBITDA. Buckets: margin expansion, cybersecurity, cheap compute (custom chips), dev infrastructure, attention.
items.angle: Classic Cisco-vs-Amazon builder/user rotation. Counterpoint: the 1,000x cost decline is deflationary for application margins too (Chegg). Moats must be data/distribution/system-of-record.
items.tweetA: Nvidia +31% in a day on a CEO reinstatement, SOXX -27% since September. When a megacap moves like a meme, that's exit liquidity, not a bottom.
items.tweetB: AI got 1,000x cheaper per unit of performance in three years. Builders' prices collapse, users' input costs collapse. A garbage hauler adding $20M EBITDA from an AI pricing tool is the 2027 trade in one sentence. $WCN
